summary: Specifies requirements for solutions supporting MPLS Network Actions (MNAs), which affect forwarding or other processing of MPLS packets. They are informed by proposals to add information to labeled packets so transit or terminating routers can perform actions.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9613 sets requirements for MPLS designs that carry instructions beyond the label normally used to forward a packet. It aims to keep those designs interoperable, efficient, and compatible with existing MPLS mechanisms.

subtitle: Requirements for adding network actions and related data to MPLS packets.

tldr.problem: MPLS forwarding normally uses the top label and Traffic Class bits. Some use cases need routers to act on other information, so solutions need shared requirements for interoperability and manageable processing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets requirements for MPLS Network Actions, Network Action Indicators, ancillary data, and the mechanism that alerts a router to their presence.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9613 is an Informational requirements document, not an MNA protocol. It leaves detailed action behavior and security design to solution specifications.

today: RFC 9613 is an Informational requirements document. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs Network Actions
sections.content:
MPLS routers traditionally make forwarding decisions using the top label and Traffic Class bits. New use cases need a general way to make forwarding or processing decisions using other information in a labeled packet. The RFC calls these operations MPLS Network Actions (MNA).

RFC 9613 specifies requirements for solutions that encode an action indicator and any associated ancillary data. It anticipates a common MNA solution and separate specifications for actions used by particular cases. This document does not define those protocols or the detailed processing of an action.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS routers usually act on a packet's top label. This RFC sets rules for future designs that let them use additional information.

sections.title: Actions, Indicators and Ancillary Data
sections.content:
A Network Action is an operation performed on an MPLS packet or because a router processed it. A Network Action Indicator (NAI) in the packet signals that an action should be performed. Ancillary Data (AD) is information associated with an action that can be used as input or produced as a result.

The RFC distinguishes in-stack data, which sits inside the MPLS label stack, from post-stack data, which sits after the bottom of that stack and before the user payload. Scope means the set of nodes that should perform a particular action.
sections.plainLanguage: An action is the operation, its indicator tells a router which operation to perform, and ancillary data supplies related information. That data can appear inside or after the MPLS label stack.

sections.title: General Requirements for Solutions
sections.content:
MNA solutions must preserve MPLS flexibility and efficiency, work with existing MPLS mechanisms, and minimize processing needed to parse the label stack. They must minimize additions to the stack and allow packets with indicators or ancillary data to share a Label Switched Path with packets that have none. A solution must not expose to transit routers information that is not already exposed to the Label Edge Router.

Specifications must discuss Equal-Cost Multipath consequences and any label-stack growth that the ingress router does not control. They must also address new security considerations. Implementations are not required to support in-stack or post-stack data unless they choose an action that uses it.
sections.plainLanguage: An MNA design must fit MPLS and keep packet processing efficient. Its specification must explain effects on routing and security, and it must coexist with packets that do not carry action information.

sections.title: Indicators, Data and Router Support
sections.content:
A solution must define how a router detects an indicator and how control and management systems learn whether downstream routers can process it. An indicator must not be sent toward a router unless that router is known to support it. A packet may carry indicators for multiple actions, although an implementation need not process all of them.

Specifications must state where indicators and ancillary data appear and whether routers may rewrite the data. The format must let routers skip indicators they do not understand. When an indicator is removed, its associated data must also be removed unless another remaining indicator needs it. The egress Label Edge Router must be told when ancillary data is present.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers need a way to know whether they can handle an action indicator. A design must also explain where related data goes and how routers can safely skip or remove it.

sections.title: Security and Information Exposure
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the MPLS forwarding plane does not provide built-in security. A solution might place information derived from the packet payload in MPLS headers, revealing data that a service user expected the network to treat as opaque.

When an upstream router inserts data that changes a downstream router's forwarding behavior, the two routers have an implicit trust relationship. Each solution specification must address the security considerations introduced by its design.
sections.plainLanguage: Information placed in MPLS headers may reveal details about packet contents. A router that acts on information inserted upstream must account for that trust relationship.
